entries.title: A write rejected with its resource version unchanged waits in NEEDS_RECONCILIATION unless fencing is on
entries.impact: Fixed in code and verified live on one host: one run each for the moved-resourceVersion and replaced-target cases on 2026-11-11 and again at 4139385 (a plain delete was not run live), and the fence for an unchanged resourceVersion at 4139385 and 5409092 (C-EXECUTOR-WEDGE-FENCE). It stays mitigated because fencing is off by default. Reconciliation is a pure decision table: a deleted or recreated target, or a resourceVersion that moved without this action's evidence, ends SUPERSEDED, which the Coordinator records as FAILED so a new proposal can follow. The live wedge harness (C-EXECUTOR-WEDGE: one run per scenario on one Windows host with kind, 2026-11-11) showed main's Executor (d5b2ed9) staying NEEDS_RECONCILIATION over 5 reconcile passes with the workload still excluded, while 4afc879 resolved the moved-resourceVersion case (rv-race) as SUPERSEDED/ADVANCED_WITHOUT_EVIDENCE and the replaced-target case (delete-recreate) as SUPERSEDED/TARGET_REPLACED, released the workload and applied a second proposal. kubectl error text is still not classified (the DEFINITE_REJECTION rows are reserved), so a rejection that leaves the same UID at the same resourceVersion, such as an admission denial, still looks like a request in flight. When fencing is configured (fence_after_seconds; off by default), a reconcile pass after the settle delay sends a metadata-only patch with the same UID and resourceVersion tests and this action's fence marker, journaled before the call. If it commits, the write never committed and never can, so the result is CONFLICT with basis FENCED and the workload is released; tests and the model checker cover it, and the model checker ends no run in doubt with fencing on. With fencing off, that action stays NEEDS_RECONCILIATION and after 600 s gets one 'Operator action required' result. Live verification of the fence (C-EXECUTOR-WEDGE-FENCE, one host, kind-sentinel-boutique-connected): in the admission-deny scenario a ValidatingAdmissionPolicy denied the template write with the same UID at the same resourceVersion; the action stayed NEEDS_RECONCILIATION before the settle delay, then one fence committed and it resolved as CONFLICT/FENCED on 5/5 reconcile passes, the workload was released and a second proposal was APPLIED. The first run (4139385) is FAILED on one harness check only, which wrongly expected metadata.generation to stay unchanged (a Deployment bumps it on an annotation change); 17d4532 fixed the check to compare the spec and the rerun at 5409092 passed every check. One run per revision; the wedge summaries carry no provenance block, so these revisions are inferred.
entries.workaround: Turn fencing on: fence_after_seconds in the Executor worker configuration, or --fence-after with runtime/live_executor.py --reconcile. With fencing off, an operator inspects the Deployment and clears the Executor ledger row by hand for the unchanged-version case. The deleted, recreated and moved-version cases need no workaround.

entries.title: A replacement Executor without the ledger row reported CONFLICT for a write that was applied
entries.impact: Fixed in code; live verification is left to P3.01 and P4.01. An Executor that finds the resourceVersion moved now looks for this action's evidence annotation on the Deployment and reports APPLIED for a peer's write without writing again. A host given a reconcile command with no ledger row journals the action as in doubt and reconciles from the proposal and live state, so it never starts that write. An execute command on a fresh host can still write, and the resourceVersion test in the patch lets at most one write for the action commit. Decision-table and integration tests cover both. One gap stays: if the peer's write was later overwritten, execute() reports CONFLICT where reconcile() reports SUPERSEDED; the Coordinator records both as FAILED. The P3.01 multi-process harness runs two Executor processes with separate ledgers and locks on one host: in S1c a peer adopted a write committed by a crashed Executor and in S2 a stalled Executor adopted its peer's write, each with one template write. That is still one machine and a file-backed test cluster; no live run has used two Executors.
entries.workaround: Run one Executor with one ledger directory, as every documented run does, until a multi-host run verifies this.

entries.title: Lifecycle ordering compared wall-clock timestamps written by different components
entries.impact: Fixed in code (P3.03); not run across machines or in kind. Worker results are now ordered by the Coordinator request they answer, not by the producers' clocks, so the wedge is gone: an answer to a superseded request gets HTTP 409 and is released, never resent for ever. Scenario S7 (both Executors on a gated test clock 300 s behind, separate processes on one Windows host, file mode, operator approval required) showed the wedge before the change (result refused with HTTP 400, incident READY). After it the result is accepted, but the Executor's own Guard re-check, which reads the same shifted clock, sees the Coordinator-stamped approval 300 s in its future and refuses: the action ends FAILED with no write and every invariant holding in 3 of 3 runs, with each Executor measuring an offset of 300.005 to 300.012 s. An Executor host whose whole clock is off by more than the bound therefore cannot complete an approved action; an in-bound peer can (S7b, 3 of 3 runs). Lease renewal now uses the lease length the Coordinator returns. Clocks still matter for freshness and expiry: the Guard tolerates a configured bound (max_clock_skew_seconds, off by default) and counts it against age and expiry; the Executor's local re-check and the Verifier's start check still compare their clock with timestamps from other processes, so skew beyond the bound ends an action FAILED or, by reading the code (no test), delays verification instead of wedging it. Workers measure their offset from the Coordinator (Cristian's algorithm) and, with a bound set, stop claiming and turn unready outside it. After a clock step this holds from the first exchange after the step: a request already claimed runs with the stepped clock until its next exchange, and a step smaller than the measurement uncertainty can go unseen. The offset is self-reported, so this guards against honest misconfiguration, not a dishonest worker. Messages accepted before store migration 4 have no high-water mark, so for an action in flight at the upgrade only the newest-request rule orders its results. Skew has only been simulated on one host, never measured between machines or in kind.
entries.workaround: Keep host clocks synchronised (NTP), and set max_clock_skew_seconds for the workers and the Guard policy and --max-clock-skew-seconds for the Coordinator, so a host past the bound stops claiming work.

entries.title: Agent mode bypasses the durable Planner journal
entries.impact: Fixed in code: agent planning now runs through prepare() and the PlannerStore journal. A model failure is retried up to three times; an abstention, a diagnosis of another component, a NO_ACTION answer or a target changed during inference ends at once. Every failure ends in a saved, delivered ESCALATE, so the incident moves to NEEDS_REVIEW, and a saved proposal replays without another model call. Still open: the planning budget applies per attempt, so one incident can use three budgets. The remote Planner worker now has an agent mode with the same hooks and journal (P3.07), tested offline only, as one OS process on one host with a fake model server. That ESCALATE guarantee covers only failures after a passed model preflight. In remote agent mode a model that is unreachable when the worker is about to claim never starts an attempt: there is no retry and no exhausted ESCALATE, and the incident stays OPEN (not NEEDS_REVIEW), its request unclaimed, until a ready agent Planner claims it. An outage that starts inside a cached preflight window (30 s by default) may use up attempts and escalate, or leave the incident OPEN once the cached check expires; which one happens depends on timing. Saved results are still re-sent while the model is down, except a proposal saved only in the Planner journal before the worker stopped, which waits for the next passed preflight. No bounded escalation for a long model outage exists (for example a Coordinator-side planning timeout); adding one is an owner decision. Verified live on one host for the harness agent mode's failure paths: from 4139385 every failed agent run ended in a saved, delivered ESCALATE with the incident in NEEDS_REVIEW and zero Executor writes, and each bundle's planning-status.json records the attempts, the error code and delivered 1. These are an off-target diagnosis at 4139385 (DIAGNOSIS_OFF_TARGET, C-AGENT-AUTOLAB-4139385), a forced 1 s planning budget that escalated BUDGET_EXCEEDED after three attempts (C-AGENT-FORCED-ESCALATION) and two abstentions at 870aa7d (C-SCENARIO-LIVE-UNSCORED). The retry after a failed model call also ran live in two passing runs: in boutique-live-20261111t221204z-602449 (C-AGENT-AUTOLAB-4139385) the Analyzer's call and in N1 at dab3b3f (boutique-live-20261112t080756z-29fd09, C-SCENARIO-LIVE-UNSCORED) the Reporter's call failed in attempt 1 after about 45 s and 2048 output tokens, and attempt 2 completed, reaching RECOVERED and the expected rule escalation respectively; each planning-status.json records 2 attempts. A lost delivery replayed after a restart has not been exercised live. Agent bundles before 4139385 predate the journal, so those failed runs left the incident OPEN.
entries.workaround: For runs recorded before this change, read the run's summary.json and dashboard event, then handle the incident by hand. The harness removes the fault as an administrator restore, which is not Sentinel recovery.

cites.text: A model that stays down does not escalate.

entries.title: No live run yet shows a person approving through the authenticated API
entries.impact: Fixed in code for the four live harness paths: the Executor experiment, Boutique walkthrough, provider mode and agent mode now create approvals through the authenticated approval API, served per run by a child process with generated tokens, and the Executor's final pre-write lookup reads them through ApprovalClient. Revocation, expiry or a stopped authority therefore fails closed with zero writes, and agent mode no longer records a pre-authorised approval. An interactive run needs a person to type the exact action ID; an unattended run must opt in to auto-lab approval, recorded under the automated-lab identity and never as a person. Agent and provider modes plan through the durable Planner journal and approve through the same session, and an agent run with --expect escalated asks for no approval and starts no authority. A Boutique run with the dashboard's lab controls can instead use ui approval: the dashboard shows the pending action, the operator types its action ID and clicks Approve or Revoke, and the dashboard server relays the decision with the run's operator credential (dashboard-operator by default); the browser holds only the lab session token, which any local process can also read, so it does not identify a person. This is proven offline with the real child process and a fake Kubernetes API, for agent mode and, since P2.04, for provider mode (run_provider_case with a real provider subprocess). Live on one host from 4139385, automated only: the connected walkthrough and the agent runs approved through the authenticated approval API in auto-lab mode, recorded under the automated-lab identity with human false (C-CONNECTED-HARNESS-AUTOLAB, C-AGENT-AUTOLAB-4139385, C-AGENT-AUTOLAB-5409092), and a reject-mode negative test stopped with one refusal, no approval and no Executor record for the refused action (C-APPROVAL-REJECT). Still no evidence shows a person approving: interactive and ui approval have not run live, and live bundles before 4139385 used pre-authorised lab approval. The file-backed negative cases still give the Executor a fixed approval record that never reaches the Coordinator; they prove refusals only. The Executor experiment's rival-process check reads a file copy of the managed record, not through ApprovalClient; the target lock refuses it before it reads the approval. The Verifier acceptance script (scripts/validation/test_verifier_connected_live.py) still calls the local approve() and reads the record straight from the store; it is outside this fix. Identities are bearer tokens over loopback HTTP, not a per-person login.
entries.workaround: Treat committed live results as pre-authorised or automated lab approval, never a person's. For new evidence of a person deciding, run with -Approval interactive (the default) and check operator_approval in summary.json.

entries.title: Sentinel's planning prompts carry log text only cleaned and quoted, and the injection gate is a pattern list no live adversarial run has exercised
entries.impact: Fixed in code; live adversarial verification pending. In agent mode, container log lines, Kubernetes event messages and incident signal details are now cleaned (control and format characters removed, NFKC applied, length capped), templated and quoted under untrusted_telemetry_evidence before a model reads them, and logs.csv keeps a cleaned copy with the hash of the raw line. A line that matches the curated instruction-like rules (override phrases, role markers, chat-template tokens, forged proposal fields, approval claims, Sentinel's own prompt headings) is withheld from every prompt: the model sees only its rule ids and hash. A code-owned gate in AgentPlanner then records an injection finding (rule ids and counts, decided_by rule) and ends the attempt in the fixed SUSPECTED_INJECTION escalation without calling the Recovery Planner, so flagged telemetry leads to ESCALATE and NEEDS_REVIEW with zero writes. The Recovery Planner no longer receives the Reporter's explanation or limitations, only cleaned prediction fields, evidence ids and quoted signals. The remote Planner worker (runtime/remote_adapters.py, OllamaProvider) runs the same rules over the raw incident signals before any model call: a flagged signal ends planning in the SUSPECTED_INJECTION escalation without a model call and the attempt's saved usage keeps the finding; otherwise its model reads the signals only quoted under untrusted_telemetry_evidence. This is proven offline with a 19-line adversarial corpus, a 26-line benign set that matches no rule, a recording scripted model and an obedient one, and for the remote worker with a recording fake Ollama server that always answers ROLLBACK and receives no request for any attack. Remaining risk: the rules are a pattern list, not a complete defence. A paraphrase they miss still reaches the model as a cleaned excerpt and can steer the diagnosis or the Recovery Planner within the Guard's limits. In agent mode the Reporter's component and reason now come from a code-owned vocabulary (L-FREE-TEXT-DECISION), so a steered diagnosis can only pick a wrong name from that list; inside the RCA agent the Analyzer's summary still reaches the Reporter. A false positive escalates a genuine incident, which is a safe failure; ordinary lines such as 'user: alice not found' or 'helm upgrade failed; action=rollback triggered' are flagged today. If an attempt on flagged telemetry fails in the model three times before its check runs, the incident ends in ATTEMPTS_EXHAUSTED and no finding is recorded. Still open: provider mode passes the raw planning context to the operator's own provider script, and the offline RCAEval CaseToolkit benchmark (agent/datasets/casetoolkit.py, not on the live path) sends upstream tool output, which can include raw log rows, to the model with no gate. Live so far with ordinary telemetry only: the eight agent runs at 870aa7d and dab3b3f (R1, R2 and N1, failures included) cleaned, quoted and gated their logs and recorded no injection finding, no rule ids and no flagged log line in any collected logs-tool result (C-INJECTION-GATE-BENIGN), so the gate raised no false positive on those logs. Live verification pending for an attack: no adversarial log line has been injected live (the harness has no step for it yet), and the remote Planner worker's gate has not run live.
entries.workaround: For a paraphrase the rules miss, the remaining controls are the Guard and authenticated approval, plus the narrow action set: in agent mode the Recovery Planner can only propose a rollback to a measured baseline, and where a provider may choose RESTART, it may only add a planner-bound restart token to the reviewed baseline template. A SUSPECTED_INJECTION escalation is a prompt for review: find the flagged lines by message_sha256 in the attempt's logs.csv and the saved observation.

entries.title: The live diagnosis was model free text and the rollback choice had no change evidence
entries.impact: Fixed in code; verified live on one host, unscored. Before this change the live diagnosis's component and reason were model free text, and the Recovery Planner could not see whether the live template differed from the baseline, so a rollback choice could not be checked against evidence. In agent mode the Reporter now picks the component from the reviewed topology plus the target and the reason from a fixed six-reason taxonomy, and must cite the ids of collected tool results that name the component. An answer outside the vocabulary gets one correction and then abstains, and a citation that does not name the component abstains. Code computes change evidence: a bounded, redacted diff of the live Pod template against the healthy baseline, image digests, rollout facts and a bound on the change's age. A code rule decides whether ROLLBACK is eligible: the reason is one a rollback can repair, the component is the target, a signal shows a rollout, startup, crash, back-off or image pull symptom, the template differs from the baseline and the change is recent. Under the default gated policy an ineligible case ends in a fixed escalation without a Recovery Planner call, a model ROLLBACK for an ineligible case is overridden, and the decision is recorded with decided_by rule or model. The rule-only and model-only policies (P1R and P3 in the replay ablation) can be chosen in the agent config for evaluation. This is proven offline with a scripted model; live as below. Remaining risk: the enum can push a confused model into a wrong but valid name; the citation check caused two live abstentions at 870aa7d, R2 and N1 (see below; a cited result that names only other components still makes the agent abstain); the change-age bound comes from the baseline time, so an old baseline refuses a genuine recent change; provider mode and the remote Planner worker's single-prompt mode do not use this context, and the remote Planner worker's agent mode (P3.07), which plans with the same AgentPlanner, has run offline only. Live on one host with qwen3:14b (three R1 runs at 870aa7d; one run per scenario at dab3b3f, and R2 and N1 once at each revision), unscored because the catalog labels are pending sign-off: at 870aa7d three standard PORT runs (R1) reached RECOVERED with component shippingservice and decided_by model (C-AGENT-R1-870AA7D). At the same revision R2 and N1 abstained although the Reporter named shippingservice: it also cited a metrics result with no findings, and the check required every cited result to name the component. That defect was fixed in ded3dcc (a cited result that names no component is neutral), merged in dab3b3f. At dab3b3f R2 reached ROLLBACK decided by the model and RECOVERED, N1 ended in ESCALATE decided by the rule with TEMPLATE_ALREADY_BASELINE and zero writes, and an R1 regression run recovered (C-SCENARIO-LIVE-UNSCORED). Those runs used the older Reporter prompt wording; 784c91a aligned it afterwards and has not run live.
entries.workaround: To let the model decide without change evidence or enforcement of the eligibility rule, set decision_policy to model in -AgentConfig; the vocabulary and citation checks still apply. A refused rollback is an escalation for review: the attempt's journal context holds the eligibility facts and the change evidence.

entries.title: Structured logs cover only the networked entrypoints, and no live run has collected them
entries.impact: Fixed in code for the networked processes: shared/log.py writes allowlisted JSON lines; the Coordinator server, worker HTTP, approval HTTP and worker service entrypoints configure it; every POST request gets one http.access line, or an auth.denied line for a 401 or 403, while GET /healthz, GET /readyz and GET requests for unknown paths (404) get none; lifecycle transitions are journalled; and every broad except handler re-raises or logs the error class, which CI enforces. Not covered: the live harnesses (the Executor wedge harness included), agent mode and the in-process pipelines that every recorded run used never configure logging, so their log events are dropped. Exception messages are never logged, only class names, by design. Since P3.02, W3C trace context follows an incident through outbox rows, claimed deliveries and worker HTTP requests, and spans are written as span.start and span.end log lines; approvals and the in-process pipelines add no spans of their own, there is no OpenTelemetry export. Distributed-scenario runs now collect each process's JSON log lines as the run's timeline.jsonl: in file mode (fake cluster) scripts/trace_view.py rebuilt S0 and S1a into one connected trace across six processes (C-TRACE-FILE-679EF29), and the kind-mode runs, which wrote to a real Deployment, kept their timelines in their bundles (C-DISTRIBUTED-KIND-ALL). From 4139385 the per-run approval authority, an approval HTTP server in its own process, served the live runs' approvals (C-CONNECTED-HARNESS-AUTOLAB) and wrote its log lines to approval-authority.log in the run folder, but the evidence profiles do not collect that log, so no committed bundle holds them. No Boutique harness or agent-mode run has collected logs yet.
entries.workaround: For recorded runs, read the per-run JSON evidence files and the dashboard event journal. For networked runs, collect each process's stderr with SENTINEL_LOG_FORMAT=json and print the traces with scripts/trace_view.py.

entries.impact: With no other failure signal, desired replicas of 0 produce no incident, so an accidental scale-down is not detected.
entries.workaround: None. Only the invalid-PORT fault is in scope today.

entries.title: The Coordinator is one process with one SQLite file
entries.impact: No replica takes over if the Coordinator host or its volume is lost; work waits until it returns. Since P3.06 a worker waits at most 15 s, with full jitter, between failed passes, instead of up to 60 s on a fixed schedule. Measured in file mode (separate processes on one Windows host, loopback, a shared and busy machine; not a cluster): after a 75 s outage the slowest of five workers claimed again 8.1 s (median of 6 restarts) after the restarted Coordinator was ready, against 56.7 s before; after a 30 s outage it was 10.4 s against 5.6 s, because the old fixed schedule happened to line up. Every claim still replays the whole pending outbox in one transaction, so claims per second fall as the backlog grows (measured on one host, not a cluster: about 40 to 55 with 50 to 200 commands queued, 21 to 23 with 1,000).
entries.workaround: Restart the Coordinator on the same volume; saved requests replay from SQLite.

entries.title: A Coordinator restored from a backup is detected, but lost acknowledged results are re-driven by hand
entries.impact: Restoring the Coordinator database from an earlier copy drops results it had already acknowledged, and workers do not resend acknowledged results by themselves. Since P3.06 the database has a random generation and a commit counter that grows with every changing transaction, every worker reply carries both, with the counter read before the request changed anything, and a worker that sees another generation, or a counter from before its request lower than one it saw before sending, stops claiming new work, answers /readyz with 503 and logs it once, across restarts, while still sending its saved results. scripts/coordinator_restore_check.py lists the acknowledged results the restored database lacks, as replay (the worker resends its saved result when it claims the same request again) or review. Because the counter from before the request is compared, the worker's own request (every claim commits) cannot hide a lost commit, so a backup lacking only the newest acknowledged result is detected. Limits: a worker notices only at its next exchange, and only if it saw a higher counter before; if a restore lost k commits and other workers' requests commit k or more times before a worker's next exchange (each idle claim counts), that worker does not notice (the check with --previous-commit still does). A worker whose Coordinator sends no store headers detects nothing. A worker restarted after the restore compares with the position at its latest acknowledged result only. The Observer's incident outbox does not watch the store, and nothing re-drives a review item. In restore drills (separate processes on one Windows host, file mode; never on a cluster) every worker stopped within 0.31 s and the check listed exactly the two lost results (those drills ran before the counter from before the request was compared, which can only make a worker notice sooner). Clearing every worker at once left the action VERIFYING in 4 of 8 drills: by our reading another Executor claimed the replayed request first and reported its own result, which the Verifier's job store refuses as a second execution for the action. Clearing the workers holding replay items first recovered 5 of 5 with no new write.
entries.workaround: Before a restore, note the commit counter of the database being replaced (SELECT commit_counter FROM store_meta); if it cannot be read because the node or volume is lost, the positions remembered in the workers' transport.db files are the only reference. Run scripts/coordinator_restore_check.py with --previous-commit and every worker's transport.db after it, re-drive or review what it lists, then clear each worker with worker_service --accept-store, those holding replay items first.

entries.title: The Executor ledger and target locks are host-local
entries.impact: The ledger and the OS lock are still per host. Since P3.04 the Coordinator gives each workload one Executor owner at a time: while an Executor holds a live lease on a command for a workload no other Executor can claim one for it, every claim gets the workload's next ownership epoch, and a result from a claim that is no longer the latest gets HTTP 409. When a claimed command is withdrawn, another Executor seals the target before anything else runs on it (L-NO-FENCING). This is tested offline and with separate processes on one host against the file-backed test cluster; no run has used Executors on separate machines or a real API server.
entries.workaround: Keep the Coordinator's per-target ownership on (it cannot be turned off); a lease alone is not a fence.

cites.text: These locks do not implement distributed leases or fencing across hosts.

entries.title: Abandoned or revoked Executor writes are fenced only by a seal, run live on one kind node
entries.impact: Revocation is still check-then-act: a kubectl patch can land up to 15 s after the Executor's last authority check, and its resourceVersion test does not stop it if nobody else wrote in between. Since P3.04, when the Coordinator withdraws a command an Executor has claimed (a revoked approval, new evidence, a new Guard decision), or a later holder reports FAILED, it queues executor.seal and blocks the workload. Another Executor reads the target and, if the version is still the one the proposal was planned on, sends a metadata-only patch with the same UID and resourceVersion tests and its ownership epoch; once that commits, the abandoned patch can never commit. A write that already landed is reported APPLIED and the incident goes to NEEDS_REVIEW, and a seal that cannot finish in 5 passes goes to review and leaves the workload blocked until an operator queues another (reseal). Shown offline with the production kubectl adapter against the file-backed test cluster: Executor A stopped at the before_patch fault point after its last checks, a revocation, Executor B's seal, and then A's patch refused with zero template writes, where the same script without the seal shows one write after the revocation; and in scenario S8 with separate processes on one host. An Executor's own fence of its write still in doubt (P2.06, the same metadata-only patch without an epoch) has run live on one host at 4139385 and 5409092 (C-EXECUTOR-WEDGE-FENCE). The seal has now run live in kind-mode S8 against the real shippingservice Deployment, 4 runs at 0a8d4d7 and be6e636 (C-SEAL-LIVE): each time the other Executor sealed at fence epoch 2 with a metadata-only patch (generation +1, no template write), the paused Executor's conditional patch was refused (CONFLICT), 0 writes landed after the release and the incident ended FAILED as expected. The Coordinator answered the paused Executor's lease renewal with HTTP 409 lease_not_current in all 4 runs, and its result with 409 result_changed in 3 of 4 (in be6e636 r2 the result_changed 409 went to guard-1, and the paused Executor logged a lost lease and retried); no stale-epoch error was seen. Those runs had no admission policy installed; the policy's epoch rule was checked separately (C-ADMISSION-POLICY-LIVE). The seal leaves sentinel.io/fence and sentinel.io/fence-epoch on the Deployment and the kind restore puts back only the template, so the operator removed them by hand after each session. Limits: it fences Pod-template writes made through the conditional patch only, assumes one linearizable etcd with resourceVersions that never repeat, keeps the workload blocked while no Executor can reach the API server, and until the seal commits a revoked write can still land (it is then reported, not prevented). RBAC limits verbs and resources, not Deployment fields; the admission policy that limits fields and refuses a lower fence epoch has passed one live check in a disposable namespace but is not installed in the lab namespaces (L-EXECUTOR-FIELD-LIMITS). Still to do: the audit-log proof (P4.01), and any run across separate machines; the S8 runs used the deterministic synthetic planner on one kind node on one host.
entries.workaround: None needed offline. For live runs, keep fencing and the seal on, and treat a NEEDS_REVIEW incident from a seal as a write that landed after revocation. After an S8 run, remove the fence annotations with a uid- and resourceVersion-tested metadata patch before the next store seals the same Deployment.

entries.title: The Executor's field limits are an admission policy checked live once but installed nowhere by default
entries.impact: RBAC limits the Executor credential to get and patch on the Deployments its Role names (one, demo-api, in executor-rbac.yaml; in the Roles the Boutique lab harness generates for its own namespaces, shippingservice alone in the single-service labs and shippingservice and cartservice in the connected lab), not to fields. P3.05 adds deploy/sentinel/executor-admission.yaml, a parameter-free ValidatingAdmissionPolicy (admissionregistration.k8s.io/v1, Kubernetes 1.30 or later) for any ServiceAccount named sentinel-executor, bound to the sentinel-demo namespace; the binding as written does not select the Boutique lab namespaces (sentinel-boutique, sentinel-boutique-connected) that hold the labs' targets. It allows a Pod template change only with a new sentinel.io/execution annotation, allows only the sentinel.io/execution, sentinel.io/fence and sentinel.io/fence-epoch annotations to be added or changed, denies removing any annotation, keeps a fence or seal metadata-only, requires the fence epoch to be a decimal integer below 10^18 that never decreases, and denies changes to replicas, labels, finalizers, ownerReferences and the other 6 DeploymentSpec fields that exist today (a field Kubernetes adds later is not held until it is added to the policy; the live check compares the server's list). It is checked structurally offline: the manifests parse, the identity and namespace match executor-rbac.yaml, each rule names its fields, each CEL expression is pinned to its reviewed text, and every patch the production adapter sends stays inside it. Its CEL has now been evaluated by a real API server once: the live check (scripts/validation/test_executor_admission_live.py at 599f44f, Kubernetes 1.37, a disposable namespace on kind-sentinel-boutique-connected with the policy bound to it) matched 24 of 24 probes: 6 allowed (a real ROLLBACK and RESTART through the production adapter, seals at epochs 5, 6 and 6, and a fence without an epoch), 12 denied by the policy with the rule named and the object unchanged, and 6 denied by RBAC (C-ADMISSION-POLICY-LIVE). Nothing installs the policy in the Boutique lab namespaces or by default, and the kind-mode scenario runs ran without it, so there RBAC is still the only enforced limit. Even when enforced it cannot limit the Pod template's content: a stolen token can still write any template, image and service account included, if it also writes an evidence annotation. A stale rollback is still fenced by the resourceVersion test, not by the epoch, which only a seal writes. Installing it has a cost for the seal: the epoch belongs to one Coordinator store (each target_ownership row starts at 1 and grows by one per claim) and the Coordinator never reads the Deployment's annotation, but sentinel.io/fence-epoch stays on the Deployment, because a ROLLBACK replaces only the Pod template. So a new, reset or restored store, such as the per-run store each live experiment run creates, cannot seal a Deployment sealed earlier at a higher epoch until its own epochs pass that value: each seal patch is denied, the adapter reports it as WriteOutcomeUnknown (it cannot tell a denial from a lost reply), the seal reads again and retries, and after 5 passes it reports UNSEALED, so the workload goes to review and stays blocked; without the policy the same seal would commit. The live check confirmed this: a seal at epoch 1 from a fresh Coordinator store was denied ('may not decrease') and the adapter reported WriteOutcomeUnknown. Any other policy denial of an Executor write is likewise reported as WriteOutcomeUnknown and settled by reconciliation from a read. Choices made while writing it, for the owners to confirm: a template change does not have to carry a fence epoch; the identity is any ServiceAccount named sentinel-executor in any namespace, while the binding limits the policy to Deployments in sentinel-demo; a malformed stored epoch fails closed and blocks every Executor write to that Deployment until an administrator fixes it; the evidence annotation may change without a template change; and the binding names no Deployment, so the Role's resourceNames picks the targets. Owner decision open: seed a store's epoch from the observed annotation, or fence by resourceVersion only and drop the epoch rule. The P4.01 acceptance harness installs the same policy, bound to its own target namespace sentinel-dist-workload with every CEL expression unchanged, and its scenario S9 expects a spec.replicas patch from the Executor to be denied; written and tested offline only, not run.
entries.workaround: Where the policy is not installed, rely on the Role's resourceNames, the 1 h token and the Guard. An administrator can apply executor-admission.yaml after executor-rbac.yaml on Kubernetes 1.30 or later; its binding selects sentinel-demo, so a lab namespace needs its own binding. With the policy installed, before a new or restored Coordinator store works on a Deployment that carries sentinel.io/fence-epoch, an administrator removes that annotation (kubectl annotate deployment <name> sentinel.io/fence-epoch-) or recreates the Deployment.

entries.title: The networked worker layer has only run on one host
entries.impact: Since P3.01 the Coordinator and every worker run as separate processes on one host, with their own state, credentials and TCP connections, under injected network, process and timing faults (CI, file-backed test cluster). That is still one machine: one kernel clock, one disk and loopback networking. The delivery layer has not run on separate nodes, and containers or kind nodes on one Docker host would still not be separate machines. Against the kind lab (one kind node on the same host), kind mode has now run in two operator sessions on 12 Nov 2026, each S1b, S1c, S2, S4, S5 and S8 twice, with the Executors patching the real shippingservice Deployment and the deterministic synthetic planner: with scratch bundle and injection tools at 0a8d4d7, 12 of 12 runs matched their expectation once the health policy was relaxed (the first attempt, under the stricter policy, failed I3; C-DISTRIBUTED-KIND-0A8D4D7); with the committed experiments/distributed/kind_bundle.py and the in-harness injection and restore at be6e636, 11 of 12 did, and S2 r2 failed I5 after its Verifier command was delivered 8 times (C-DISTRIBUTED-KIND-BE6E636, L-VERIFIER-RETRY-BACKOFF). Every run's invariants otherwise held, with 0 unobserved windows (C-DISTRIBUTED-KIND-ALL). A worker image for every role (P3.07) has been built and scanned locally, and an agent-mode Planner ran from it as a container against a Coordinator on the host at be6e636 and stayed ready through an 89.6 s planning pass, reaching qwen3:14b on the host's Ollama over plain HTTP with allow_insecure_remote set (C-WORKER-CONTAINER-READINESS); the topology cannot yet start a worker as a container. All of this is processes and containers on one machine, not separate nodes. P4.01 adds the groundwork for a four-node kind lab, sentinel-dist (deploy/kind/kind-dist.yaml with an API server audit policy, deploy/sentinel/sentinel-dist with the Coordinator and every worker as its own Deployment, Secret and PVC, the Coordinator and the two Executors pinned to three different nodes, and per-worker NetworkPolicy), and an acceptance harness (experiments/distributed/kind_acceptance.py) for scenarios S0-S9 with Chaos Mesh and docker pause that counts template writes from the audit log (I7). It is written and tested offline only: the cluster has never been created, no worker has run in a Pod, and the results table in docs/distributed-acceptance.md is empty. Even when it runs, its four nodes are containers on one Docker host, sharing one kernel, clock and disk.

entries.title: A worker's /readyz turned 503 during a long pass while it was renewing its lease
entries.impact: Found live on 12 Nov 2026: an agent-mode Planner container that was planning normally failed two Docker health checks during one 128.7 s planning pass (C-WORKER-READINESS-BEFORE-FIX; Docker kept it healthy only because three failures in a row are needed), because /readyz counted only the end of a polling pass as Coordinator contact and turned 503 once that was older than --ready-seconds (60), although the worker renewed its lease every few seconds. A liveness-style probe on /readyz would have killed a healthy Planner mid-inference. Fixed in code: every Coordinator request answered with 200 (a claim, each lease renewal, a result, a clock measurement) now counts as contact, a refused, failed or timed-out request never does, and --ready-seconds must be longer than the 5 s renewal interval; the preflight, clock and store conditions are unchanged. The trade-off: a worker whose own component fails on every pass (an Executor that cannot reach its cluster, a Planner whose model call crashes after its preflight passed) still has its claims and retries answered, so it now stays ready; that shows only in its retry and back-off log lines. The fix has now run once in a container (C-WORKER-CONTAINER-READINESS): an image built at be6e636 planned an R1 incident in one 89.6 s pass, longer than the 60 s window, and all 88 health samples from the first Docker-healthy one until the Coordinator stopped were Docker healthy with /readyz 200 (89 were taken while it was up; the first, still starting, also answered /readyz 200), with the highest contact age 19.1 s (during a worker.status retry after a TimeoutError at 18:24:31, after the pass). After the Coordinator stopped, /readyz answered 503 at 62.0 s, one readiness window, but Docker's status turned unhealthy only at 126.0 s, because the image's HEALTHCHECK runs every 30 s and needs 3 failures. Lease renewals during the pass are inferred from the single-attempt receipt; the Coordinator logs no renew line at info level. It stays mitigated: one run on one host.
entries.workaround: Before the fix: a --ready-seconds longer than the longest model call, or a container HEALTHCHECK that is not used to restart the worker. With the fix, poll /readyz directly when a failed Coordinator must be noticed within one readiness window; Docker's health status lags it by up to three 30 s checks.

entries.title: In kind mode the Coordinator's retry back-off spaced the Verifier's samples past the health policy's gap
entries.impact: Fixed in code; live verification pending. Found live in kind mode at be6e636 (S2 r2, C-DISTRIBUTED-KIND-BE6E636): the Executor's rollback committed and the template went back to baseline, but the Verifier ended FAILED and invariant I5 failed because its command was delivered 8 times, above MAX_ATTEMPTS (6). The live Verifier then took one sample per pass and gave the delivery back while the target was not yet healthy; the Coordinator offered it again after a back-off that doubles per attempt (1, 2, 4, ... up to 60 s), so passes came at about +1, +2.6, +5.1, +9.7, +18.3, +34.9, +67.5 and +127.7 s after the write. The kind policy distributed-kind-lab-2 needs 2 samples no more than 20 s apart within a 60 s convergence grace and a 90 s timeout, so once the gaps passed 20 s a target that became healthy late could not be confirmed. The cause is inferred: the run kept no record of when the rollout became Available or of the Verifier's own samples. I5 also had no margin in kind mode: the Verifier command took 5 or 6 attempts in each of the 9 passing non-S8 runs. The first kind attempt at 0a8d4d7, under a stricter policy (3 samples, 10 s gap, 60 s deadline), failed I3 with the incident still VERIFYING at the deadline, which is why the policy was relaxed; that it failed through the same back-off is inferred, because its records show only the I3 failure and at most 6 attempts per command. Seen with a single kind node on one host while other test sessions shared it; not seen in file mode. The fix: a remote Verifier pass now keeps its claim and samples until the evidence is conclusive, one reading every sampling_interval seconds (at most half of max_sample_gap_seconds; 10 s under distributed-kind-lab-2, which is unchanged), checking its lease before every reading and at least once a second while waiting, until the store freezes an outcome, at the latest at the fixed deadline; a pass gives the delivery back after at most 600 s. A lost lease stops sampling and posts no result, and readings survive a crash, so a re-delivered command continues from them against the same deadline. Offline, on a simulated clock with the real delivery layer and the kind policy, the be6e636 timeline (target healthy from +40 s) now ends RECOVERED after one delivery at about +51 s; the same test on the code before the fix ends FAILED after 8 deliveries. File-mode S0 and S2 now require at most 2 Verifier deliveries (1 observed), and each run's summary.json records the Verifier's readings (seconds after the write and each one's status) and verifier_attempts. Not re-run in kind mode. Residual: a Verifier down for longer than about the gap minus the interval (10 s here) after the target turned healthy leaves a gap the rules count, and the verdict then fails closed (FAILED, or NEEDS_REVIEW) at the deadline instead of confirming recovery.
entries.workaround: Until kind mode has been re-run (S2 and S8, --repeat 2), read a kind-mode Verifier FAILED after a committed rollback against that run's summary.json: verification gives when each Verifier reading was taken and its status, and verifier_attempts how often the command was delivered. On a build before this fix, treat such a FAILED as possibly a sampling artefact and check the target's rollout and health directly before treating it as a failed recovery.

entries.title: A crashed Executor whose peer finished the action kept it in doubt and refused that workload
entries.impact: Fixed in code (P3.04); not run in kind or across machines. Found by the P3.01 harness (S1b and S1c): an Executor killed after journalling its write intent, or after its patch, kept the action WRITE_STARTED when its peer finished the action, because no command for it reached the crashed host again; that host would then refuse later actions on the workload with TargetBusy. entries.title: The restart budget is kept per Executor ledger, and only local wiring gives it to the Guard
entries.impact: The Guard counts a target's recent restarts from live_state.restart_history, which the Executor reads from its own SQLite ledger under the target lock, so the budget survives an Executor restart. It supplies only the newest 1000 restarts, which is enough to decide any allowed budget (at most 100 per window). Executors on other hosts keep separate ledgers, so each host would have its own budget. The Boutique live harnesses (operator, provider, agent and Chaos Mesh modes) now give their Coordinator-side Guard pass the history from the run's own Executor ledger, so a RESTART there is checked against its budget instead of escalating as RESTART_BUDGET_UNKNOWN; this is tested offline only, and each run starts a new ledger, so the budget does not carry from one run to the next. The HTTP Guard worker and the Kubernetes state reader of scripts/coordinator.py (runtime/guard_pipeline.py KubectlStateReader) still do not supply the history, so a RESTART through either escalates as RESTART_BUDGET_UNKNOWN.
entries.workaround: Run one Executor per target, as every committed run does. Treat RESTART as tested offline only.

entries.title: Two simultaneous faults are implemented and tested offline only
entries.impact: Fixed in code; live verification pending. Concurrent incidents queue per workload, and P4.05 adds two catalog pairs run with --pair on the connected lab: an independent pair (shipping invalid PORT, ROLLBACK, and a cart Chaos Mesh pod failure, RESTART) and a dependency-ordered pair (a redis-cart pod failure, RESTART, and a cart REDIS_ADDR rollout, ROLLBACK). Each pair target is verified by its own probe and the readiness of the services it calls, never by its callers or the storefront, so one broken service can no longer mark the other target's correct repair NOT_RECOVERED; the storefront is judged separately as a ShopOutcome (RECOVERED, PARTIAL, FAILED or UNKNOWN) that never changes an incident's state. Single-target runs keep the whole-shop verification. A repair the Guard refuses with DEPENDENCY_BLOCKED because the other pair target is down is planned again once, only after that target is RECOVERED; refusals that name each other stop both incidents with no write (DEPENDENCY_DEADLOCK), and any other refusal, escalation or refused approval stops that incident only. Offline, with the real Coordinator, Guard, Executor and Verifier against fake Deployments, both incidents reach READY together with one write each and no incident changes state because of the other. With a cart that stays Ready, the blocked cart repair is REJECTED and then ALLOWed after Redis RECOVERED with exactly one write; with the faulted cart NotReady, as in the live C1 runs, the Guard refuses both repairs and the pair stops with DEPENDENCY_DEADLOCK and no write. The harness's own verdict checks (cross-incident transitions, an early cart ALLOW, write counts other than one per target, an accepted changed payload under a reused action ID, a reconciliation that writes, a killed worker that did not stop after its write) are tested offline with fakes. Nothing has run on a cluster: the live recipe (docs/dual-fault.md), including the Executor-kill variant and the timing comparison with single-fault runs, is not run, and the pair labels need sign-off. With the Guard's dependency rule as it stands, the dependency-ordered pair is predicted to stop with DEPENDENCY_DEADLOCK, which the catalog accepts as a safe stop but which is not evidence of an ordered recovery (L-CALLER-BLOCKS-CALLEE-REPAIR). redis-cart is a third, pair-only target: its pair's Executor Role, allowlist and approval authority name it, and a Redis restart empties the lab's cart data. One harness process drives both incidents and collects one target's verification window at a time, on one host, so pair timings do not measure independent workers. The cart and Redis pod failures have no single-run form to compare against. Arbitrary N-fault recovery is not claimed.
entries.workaround: Quote no pair result until the live recipe in docs/dual-fault.md has run with signed-off labels; until then inject one fault per run for live claims. Never quote a DEPENDENCY_DEADLOCK run as an ordered recovery: check ordered_recovery_shown in pair-result.json.

entries.title: A callee cannot be repaired while a caller it broke is NotReady, so the dependency-ordered pair cannot show its ordering
entries.impact: The Guard's dependency finding covers every service that reaches the target or that the target reaches, and any one that is not ready refuses the repair with DEPENDENCY_BLOCKED. A callee whose outage makes its caller NotReady therefore cannot be repaired while that caller is NotReady. In the P4.05 dependency-ordered pair (redis-pod+cart-config) the C1 cart fault leaves the cart Pod NotReady, as the live C1 runs show, so the Redis RESTART is refused because of cartservice and the cart ROLLBACK because of redis-cart: the refusals name each other and the run stops with DEPENDENCY_DEADLOCK and no write. That is a safe stop, and the catalog pre-registers it as acceptable, but it is not evidence that the cart ALLOW came after Redis RECOVERED, which P4.05 asks for. The ordered recovery has been shown offline only with a cart that stays Ready. Whether a Redis outage on its own also makes cartservice NotReady, so that a lone Redis failure would be blocked too, has not been run. Changing the rule is a safety decision for the owner, with a written argument and a failing-then-passing test; docs/dual-fault.md lists the options.
entries.workaround: Report a DEPENDENCY_DEADLOCK pair run as a safe stop with no ordered recovery shown, and keep the P4.05 ordering check and the Phase 4 dual-fault exit item open until the owner decides.

entries.title: Model cold loads make agent planning slow and variable
entries.impact: Incident-to-repair time in agent mode had a long tail (docs/results.md). The two measured cold calls took up to 41 s with model loads up to 26 s, and one 356 s decision stage holds only 53 s of recorded model calls, so its cause is not established. The bounded transport is in code: each model call has an overall deadline, a response size cap, no redirects or proxies and a schema check; agent mode runs a preflight and a warm-up call before any fault is injected and records model-runtime.json; keep_alive is configurable. Measured live on 4afc879 (C-AGENT-RECORDED: three runs on one Windows host, 2026-11-11): with qwen3:14b Q4_K_M fully on the GPU and keep_alive 30m, all nine model calls were warm (load under 1 s), model time per run was 21.9 to 24.0 s and incident to Guard ALLOW took 23.3 to 25.6 s; the first run's warm-up loaded the model in 18.6 s before the fault was injected. The preflight stopped a missing model before fault injection (C-AGENT-PREFLIGHT-RECORDED). Not measured: a cold load during a run with the bounded transport, so the tail after an evicted or cold model is unknown. The per-call timeout still defaults to 300 s; P2.01 puts agent planning under a planning budget.
entries.workaround: Keep the model warm with keep_alive and check the warm-up load time in model-runtime.json after each run.

entries.impact: Fixed in code; live verification pending. Three catalog scenarios now drive guarded recovery with Chaos Mesh, in kind-sentinel-boutique-connected only. N2 is a pod failure where RESTART is correct; the run passes only with an attribution proof that the restarted Pod was not one the fault selected, that it recovered at least 60 s before the fault expired, and that the same chaos object was still running afterwards. N3 is CPU stress; a read-only metrics-server bridge feeds the Observer's thresholds, raises no alert unless every owned Pod has complete metrics, and a Planner rule escalates a metric-only incident before any provider or model call. T1 is a network delay where no incident is correct, recorded only with a true-negative proof. In each run a forced wrong action goes to the Executor with no approval, and the Executor's own Guard check must refuse it with zero writes: ROLLBACK during the pod failure, RESTART during a template drift and RESTART during CPU stress (in N3 also when no incident opens; N3's label scores NO_INCIDENT acceptable, and that run continues only with a passing true-negative proof). A REJECT with any other reason code, and a forced action that unexpectedly passes every check (escalated for approval, nothing written), both fail the run. A chaos run refuses any --expect that contradicts its label, so a trial whose label expects no repair never asks for approval. Setup is install only: the Chaos Mesh 2.8.2 chart with namespace filtering and metrics-server pinned by chart version and image digest; any other context and any sentinel-lab name are refused, and so is a context whose only node is not the connected lab's. The Chaos Mesh controller and daemon images come from the chart's default tags, not digests, and the metrics-server digest is supplied at install time and not yet committed. All of this is tested offline against fakes; nothing has run on a cluster and the labels still need sign-off. The Chaos Mesh record format (namespace/pod ids and desiredPhase), whether Chaos Mesh re-selects a restarted Pod, and whether CPU stress crosses the 0.18-core threshold are assumptions until the spike. In agent mode the Recovery Planner cannot choose RESTART, so the agent variant of N2 can at best escalate. The separate chaos demonstration runner still takes no recovery action. The HTTP fault needs a kernel module the Docker Desktop WSL2 kernel lacks, and the DNS fault needs a shell the hardened Boutique pods do not have.
entries.workaround: Quote no Chaos Mesh recovery result until the live recipe in docs/chaos.md has run with signed-off labels. Until then use the demonstration runner's CPU, memory, Pod and network faults as injection demonstrations only.

cites.text: DNSChaos needs a shell and a writable /etc

entries.title: Most committed evidence has inferred provenance
entries.impact: Bundles collected before provenance stamping carry a best-guess revision: every chaos, security-lab, observer, packaged, shipping-lab, provider-recovery and ui-session bundle, the four earlier connected-harness runs, the two earlier Guard rejections and 20 agent runs. Recorded bundles now exist for the cited live classes: one connected-harness run, one Guard rejection with zero Executor patch attempts and four agent runs from 4afc879 on 2026-11-11 (C-CONNECTED-HARNESS-RECORDED, C-GUARD-REJECTION-RECORDED, C-AGENT-RECORDED, C-AGENT-PREFLIGHT-RECORDED), plus the offline Guard evaluation. The Phase 2 live runs of 2026-11-11 and 2026-11-12 add 18 recorded bundles at 4139385, 5409092, 870aa7d and dab3b3f: two connected-harness runs, one Guard rejection and 15 agent runs (C-CONNECTED-HARNESS-AUTOLAB, C-AGENT-AUTOLAB-5409092, C-SCENARIO-LIVE-UNSCORED and others). The seven Executor wedge bundles are inferred: the harness summary has no provenance block, so each revision is the operator's statement in the MANIFEST basis. The Phase 3 runs of 2026-11-12 add 4 recorded bundles at b79fb5d and a932a5f (three connected-harness runs and one agent run; C-CART-TARGET-LIVE, C-SHIPPING-REGRESSION-B79FB5D) and 32 inferred ones: 27 distributed-scenario runs, whose summary stamps git_revision but no dirty flag or tool versions, two kind lab sessions, the admission policy check and two worker-container runs, whose revisions are operator statements. The kind-mode runs at 0a8d4d7 were also driven by scratch tools that were never committed. Every live run is on one Windows host, and no release tag ties the evidence to a frozen artefact.
entries.workaround: Quote each claim with its scope caveat, which names its provenance, and prefer the claims whose bundles are recorded.

entries.title: No tagged, scanned release image
entries.impact: The packaged runner is built locally from the checkout. It was rebuilt and scanned for PR #98, but no image is tagged or published, and that scan is not a committed evidence bundle. A release preflight, a tag-triggered build with a Trivy gate, SBOMs and checksums now exist (docs/release.md) but have not run: no tag has been pushed, and the launcher still names the 0.3.0 runner.
entries.workaround: Build the runner from the revision you are testing.

entries.title: Security lab certificates are two-day fixtures with no rotation
entries.impact: Certificates expire after two days and are not rotated, revoked or bound to a workload identity.
entries.workaround: Recreate the lab for each session.

entries.title: The Verifier judged NOT_RECOVERED on its first reading after a patch
entries.impact: A repair that worked was recorded as failed while gRPC clients were still reconnecting, so agent runs ended NOT_RECOVERED.
entries.workaround: Not needed; an opt-in convergence grace sets aside only a leading run of unhealthy readings.

entries.title: An executor.reconcile command was processed as a new execution
entries.impact: A reconcile command could start a write instead of only inspecting a journaled one.
entries.workaround: Not needed.

cites.text: A reconcile command may only inspect a write, never start one.

entries.title: The Guard held a SQLite write lock across kubectl and passed target names unchecked
entries.impact: A slow cluster read blocked other workers for up to 30 s, and a target name could be parsed by kubectl as an option.
entries.workaround: Not needed.

entries.title: Agent planning failures were not shown on the dashboard or in summary.json
entries.impact: A failed agent run looked like a stalled one, and Ollama's own error text was discarded. The incident also stayed OPEN until agent planning moved into the journal; see L-AGENT-JOURNAL.
entries.workaround: Not needed.

cites.text: Agent planning stopped; no repair proposed

entries.title: The documented Chaos Mesh network, Pod and DNS scenarios could not run as written
entries.impact: Chaos Mesh rejected the network scenario, the Pod fault run was always marked failed, and the DNS fault could not work on the hardened pods.
entries.workaround: Not needed; DNS is now refused before any cluster work.

entries.title: One failed kubectl read during Verifier sampling aborted the pass
entries.impact: A single transient read error ended verification with no outcome.
entries.workaround: Not needed.

entries.title: The packaged runner failed on a UTF-8 console
entries.impact: A byte-order mark before the image stream made the image import fail on code page 65001.
entries.workaround: Not needed.

entries.title: Lab scripts left the user's kubectl context changed or unset
entries.impact: Creating and deleting lab clusters in the default kubeconfig left the user's context pointing elsewhere or unset. Follow-up fixes for the other launchers are PRs #95 and #96.
entries.workaround: Not needed.
